title: Checkpoint: The Silent Screen
objective: After this level you can explain how silent films grew into a full art of image, gesture and music before sound arrived.
summary: Only about a quarter of American silent features survive in any form; the chapter traced silent film from nickel storefronts to palaces, Hollywood, Expressionism, montage and documentary.

cards.headline: Chapter 2 finale: most American silent features are gone.
cards.body: Of the American feature films made from 1912 to 1929, about three in four are lost. The art this chapter described can only be partly watched today. Here's why, plus the whole chapter in one breath.

events.label: A nickel theater opens in Pittsburgh
Edison's and other companies form the patent Trust
Alice Guy founds Solax in the United States
The Birth of a Nation; Hollywood is the center of US film

cards.headline: Why so many films vanished
cards.body: A 2013 study by historian David Pierce for the Library of Congress found that only 14 percent of American features from 1912 to 1929 survive complete on 35mm as released, and another 11 percent in foreign versions or lesser formats. Nitrate film is vulnerable to fire and decay, and the industry often neglected or destroyed its prints and negatives. Once sound arrived, silent features quickly disappeared from sight.

cards.headline: The whole chapter in one breath
cards.body: Thousands of nickel theaters made movies an everyday outing, and exchanges rented them films. Filmmakers left the Trust behind for Hollywood's sun and cheap land. Alice Guy filmed made-up stories; Griffith refined the close-up while his biggest film glorified the Klan. Chaplin mixed slapstick with poignancy, and Keaton kept a stone face. Palaces added music, Caligari painted its shadows, Eisenstein collided shots, and Flaherty staged real life.

cards.headline: Chapter 2 complete
learned: How silent films grew from nickel storefront shows into an art of image, gesture and music.
Why filmmakers moved to Hollywood, and which reason historians hedge.
What Griffith refined, and why The Birth of a Nation is condemned for its racism.
How Expressionist sets, Soviet montage and Nanook's staging each shaped what film could show.

questions.prompt: What share of American feature films from 1912 to 1929 survive complete on 35mm as released?

options.label: About 90 percent
options.rationale: Far fewer survive: most are lost.

options.label: About half
options.rationale: Only about a quarter survive in any form.

options.label: Only 14 percent
None at all
options.rationale: Some survive, including 14 percent complete in original form.

questions.explanation: The 2013 study found only 14 percent survive complete on 35mm as released, and 11 percent in other versions.

questions.prompt: Why did so many American silent features disappear?

options.label: Nitrate film burned and decayed, and studios neglected or destroyed prints
The Trust ordered every silent film destroyed in 1918
options.rationale: The Trust was dissolved in 1918; it destroyed no films.

options.label: Copyright law banned keeping old films
options.rationale: The level blames nitrate stock and neglect.

options.label: They were all printed on paper, which faded
options.rationale: Paper prints are how some earlier films survived.

questions.explanation: The losses are blamed on nitrate film's vulnerability to fire and decay and the industry's neglect or destruction of prints and negatives.

questions.prompt: From Level 17: besides the style, what practical reason led Caligari's makers to paint light and shadow onto the sets?

options.label: Film stock could not record real shadows
options.rationale: Real shadows could be filmed; paint saved power.

options.label: Electric power was rationed in postwar Germany
The actors refused to work under lamps
options.rationale: Nothing in the level says so.

options.label: The Trust controlled all studio lights
options.rationale: The Trust was American and controlled patents.

questions.explanation: Painting light and shadow heightened the style and saved electric power, which was rationed in postwar Germany.

questions.prompt: From Level 15: what nickname did Buster Keaton's unsmiling face earn him?

options.label: The Little Tramp
The Man of a Thousand Faces
options.rationale: Keaton was known for one expression, not many.

options.label: The Great Stone Face
The King of Comedy
options.rationale: The level gives a different nickname.

questions.explanation: Keaton was known as the Great Stone Face for performing stunts without a smile.

questions.prompt: Some films from before 1912 survive as paper prints (Level 10). Why could those outlast many later silent features?

options.label: Paper prints were projected more often, so they were copied more
options.rationale: Paper prints were copyright records, not projection copies.

options.label: They were paper deposits at the Library of Congress, not nitrate kept by studios
Early films were all shot in color
options.rationale: Nothing in either level says so.

options.label: Sound films were made on paper
options.rationale: Sound films used film stock, and silent features vanished after sound arrived.

questions.explanation: Paper prints went to the Library of Congress for copyright, while many later features were nitrate prints the industry neglected or destroyed.
